Paper Title: Reiterative Chiral Resolution/Racemization/Recycle (RRR Synthesis) for an Effective and Scalable Process for the Enantioselective Synthesis of a Dual IDO1/TDO2 Inhibitor Imidazoisoindole Derivative
Problem_Description: The organocatalytic cascade deprotection/intramolecular aza‑Michael reaction of substrate 5 gave only modest yields and poor enantioselectivity (13 % ee) even when 1 equiv of the chiral phosphoric acid (CPA) I was used; higher loadings did not improve the outcome.
Solution_Description: Replacing the expensive CPA I with cheap l‑(+)-tartaric acid (acid II) afforded quantitative conversion of the cascade (yield ≈ 100 %) although the ee remained low; this change demonstrated that a simple, inexpensive acid can drive the reaction to completion, eliminating the low‑yield problem.
Supporting_Evidence: “Acceptable yields were obtained only when at least 1 equiv of I was used. Some enantioselection (13 % ee) was observed… the cheap l-(+)-tartaric acid II furnished the desired product in a quantitative yield, even if with low ee.”

Paper Title: Reiterative Chiral Resolution/Racemization/Recycle (RRR Synthesis) for an Effective and Scalable Process for the Enantioselective Synthesis of a Dual IDO1/TDO2 Inhibitor Imidazoisoindole Derivative
Problem_Description: The original process isolated the target enantiomer by supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC), which was judged too expensive for commercial‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A fractional‑crystallization resolution using a diastereomeric salt of the racemate with 2,3‑dibenzoyl‑d‑tartaric acid was developed, removing the need for SFC and providing a scalable, cost‑effective purification.
Supporting_Evidence: “Supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC) was originally used… estimated too expensive for commercial‑scale production… the chiral resolution… via fractional crystallization allowed to produce (S)‑4 in high enantiomeric purity and good yield.”

Paper Title: Reiterative Chiral Resolution/Racemization/Recycle (RRR Synthesis) for an Effective and Scalable Process for the Enantioselective Synthesis of a Dual IDO1/TDO2 Inhibitor Imidazoisoindole Derivative
Problem_Description: Screening of chiral acids/solvents showed that most salt combinations either remained fully soluble or precipitated as near‑racemic mixtures, giving low enantiomeric excess and poor isolation.
Solution_Description: The combination of 2,3‑dibenzoyl‑d‑tartaric acid with acetone (or acetonitrile) gave significant ee (84.9 % and 64.3 %). The optimized crystallization used a 9:1 acetone/water mixture (10 mL g⁻¹), an equimolar amount of resolving agent, and cooling to –15 °C to induce selective precipitation of the desired diastereomer, delivering >99 % ee on kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the presence of 2,3‑dibenzoyl‑d‑tartaric acid in acetone or acetonitrile, encouraging chiral purities of 84.91 and 64.30 % … The best results were obtained using 10 mL of acetone/water mixture (9/1 v/v) per gram … isolating the salt at −15/–20 °C … a single crystallization … gave the target with an enantiomer excess higher than 99.0 %.”

Paper Title: Reiterative Chiral Resolution/Racemization/Recycle (RRR Synthesis) for an Effective and Scalable Process for the Enantioselective Synthesis of a Dual IDO1/TDO2 Inhibitor Imidazoisoindole Derivative
Problem_Description: Initial racemization attempts led to degradation products when run for extended periods or at high dilution, and the process required an excessively long reaction time to reach completion.
Solution_Description: A robust racemization protocol was established using 0.1 M NaOH (1.8 equiv) in 75 % ethanol (10 vol) at reflux (72 °C) for 8 h, which completed racemization without detectable degradation and could be applied at 164 g and 18.8 kg scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “With NaOH (0.1 M) as the base and 75 % ethanol as the solvent (10 volumes)… the racemization goes to completion in 8 h at reflux temperature (72 °C). Under these conditions formation of degradation products was minimized.”

Paper Title: Reiterative Chiral Resolution/Racemization/Recycle (RRR Synthesis) for an Effective and Scalable Process for the Enantioselective Synthesis of a Dual IDO1/TDO2 Inhibitor Imidazoisoindole Derivative
Problem_Description: After chiral resolution, a substantial amount of the undesired (R)‑enantiomer remained in the mother liquor, representing waste and lowering the overall material efficiency.
Solution_Description: An RRR (resolution–racemization–recycle) strategy was implemented: the recovered (R)‑4 was racemized under the optimized conditions and fed back into the resolution step, raising the overall isolated yield of (S)‑4 to 72 % (scale 1) and 71 % (scale 2).
Supporting_Evidence: “The chiral resolution combined with the recovery of the partially resolved (R)‑4 and its racemization constitutes an efficient integrated RRR process… overall yield… 72.8 % for the trial at 164 g scale … 71.3 % for the scale‑up to 18.8 kg.”

Paper Title: Reiterative Chiral Resolution/Racemization/Recycle (RRR Synthesis) for an Effective and Scalable Process for the Enantioselective Synthesis of a Dual IDO1/TDO2 Inhibitor Imidazoisoindole Derivative
Problem_Description: During the crystallization step, heating the suspension above 58 °C caused complete dissolution of the precipitate, preventing solid formation.
Solution_Description: The temperature profile was carefully controlled: heating to 75 °C externally while keeping the internal temperature ≤ 58 °C, followed by a controlled cooling ramp to –15 °C and a 16 h hold, ensuring selective precipitation of the diastereomeric salt.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction mixture was heated to +75 °C (external temperature; the internal temperature should not exceed 58 °C to avoid complete dissolution of the precipitate)… then cooled from +75 to −15 °C… and left at −15 °C for 16 h.”

Problem_Description: The previously reported Mori synthesis of oxo‑tomaymycin required 14 steps, used genotoxic MOMCl (step 3) and toxic osmium tetroxide (step 9), and generated the undesired (Z)‑olefin that needed a four‑step sequence to isomerise, making the route long, unsafe and expensive for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A concise six‑step synthesis was designed starting from commercially available Boc‑l‑Pro(4‑oxo) and employing a Wittig‑type olefination, amide coupling, TiCl₃‑mediated chemoselective nitro reduction/cyclisation and a final acidic debenzylation, thereby eliminating the hazardous reagents and shortening the sequence.
Supporting_Evidence: “From a development point of view, their synthesis presents significant challenges, such as length (14 steps … and the use of genotoxic MOMCl (step 3) and toxic osmium derivative (OsO₄, step 9) …” (p. 2‑3) | “The present article has described a six‑step synthesis … amenable to decagram‑scale synthesis.” (p. 15) | “The most notable feature of this work is the chemoselective reduction of nitro compound 14 mediated by TiCl₃ …” (p. 15)

Problem_Description: The literature Wittig conditions (THF, t‑BuOK, reflux) failed to give the expected vinylidene product 10; no product was observed and the reaction gave poor conversion.
Solution_Description: A rapid screening was performed; the optimal protocol used t‑BuOK (1 M in THF) as base, MTBE as solvent, and a pre‑formed phosphorane before addition of 9, providing 89 % isolated yield (E/Z = 1.4).
Supporting_Evidence: “Step 1 was evaluated, based on the literature precedent. Problem_Description: The Wittig reaction produced a 1 : 1 mixture of (E)‑ and (Z)‑isomers of 10, which reduced the amount of desired (E)‑isomer available for downstream steps and required separation.
Solution_Description: The crude (E/Z) mixture was isolated as an MTBE solution and later the pure (E)‑11 was obtained after chromatographic separation (initially by SFC, then by HPLC for higher productivity).
Supporting_Evidence: “10 was obtained as a 1/1 ratio of E and Z isomers … the two isomers could be easily separated later in the synthesis (vide supra).” (p. 7) | “The mixture … was purified by chromatography. Problem_Description: During N‑Boc deprotection, an ethyl‑ester impurity (E‑12′) formed (up to 8.1 % surface area) because residual HCl in MeOH led to acidic degradation of EtOAc during the solvent‑swap step, causing trans‑esterification.
Solution_Description: A preliminary distillation was introduced to remove excess HCl before the solvent swap, and the reaction was performed in i‑PrOAc (more stable toward trans‑esterification) and later in CH₂Cl₂, reducing the impurity to 2 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “The root cause of the formation of this ethyl ester impurity was traced back to the solvent swap step (MeOH → EtOAc)… To circumvent this problem, a preliminary distillation step was performed … the amount of (E‑12′) dropped from 8.1 % to an acceptable 2 %.” (p. 11‑12) | “Conducting this reaction in isopropyl acetate … did not lead to clean crystallization …” (p. 12)

Problem_Description: The amide coupling of 12 with 13 using traditional reagents required DMF (a mutagenic solvent) and HOBt (potentially explosive), and gave only modest yields (~63 %).
Solution_Description: The coupling was carried out in 2‑MeTHF using CMPI (Mukaiyama’s reagent) and DIPEA, delivering 95 % isolated yield on ~400 mmol scale, avoiding DMF and HOBt.

Problem_Description: Alternative nitro‑reduction methods (FeSO₄, Na₂S₂O₄, Pt/C) gave low yields of the cyclised product or required up to 3.5 days, making the step inefficient for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: TiCl₃ (8 equiv) in AcOH/2‑MeTHF at 20 °C effected fast (≤5 h) chemoselective reduction and spontaneous cyclisation, affording 87 % isolated yield of 15.
